title: How to Remove Hard Water Stains From Glass Shower Doors
metaTitle: How to Remove Hard Water Stains From Shower Glass | Las Cruces
metaDescription: Mineral spots on shower glass need dwell time, not scrubbing. The vinegar method, what to keep acid away from, and how to tell when glass is etched.
summary: Spots on shower glass aren't dirt, and scrubbing harder is why most people give up on them.
transcript: Hard water spots on shower glass aren't dirt. They're mineral deposits, mostly calcium and magnesium, left behind when a drop of water evaporates and the minerals in it don't. That's why scrubbing harder doesn't work. You're not moving soil, you're trying to abrade rock off glass.
Start with white vinegar, undiluted. Warm it a little if you can, because warm acid works faster. Put it in a spray bottle and soak the glass until it's visibly wet, not misted.

The part people skip is dwell time. Give it ten to fifteen minutes, and re-wet the glass whenever it starts to dry. Vinegar only works while it's liquid and in contact with the deposit. A quick spray and wipe does almost nothing, which is how most people conclude vinegar doesn't work on their shower.

On a vertical door the spray won't hold. Lay paper towels or a cloth against the glass and soak those. They keep the vinegar in place long enough to matter instead of letting it run straight into the pan.

After the dwell, work the glass with a white non-scratch pad. Not green, and not steel wool. Both will scratch glass, and scratches hold minerals better than smooth glass does, so a scratched door gets worse every time you clean it.
Rinse completely, then squeegee dry. The rinse matters because leftover vinegar residue builds a film of its own.

If a haze survives two rounds, the deposit has been there long enough to start etching. At that point move to a mild abrasive polish made for glass, or an oxalic acid cleaner like Bar Keepers Friend, worked wet with the same white pad. Test a low corner first.

Know when to stop. True etching is physical damage to the glass surface, not a deposit sitting on top of it, and no cleaner removes it. Run a wet finger over the haze. If it still looks cloudy while it's wet, it's etched, and the fix is a polishing compound or a new panel.

Two things to keep acid away from. Natural stone, including marble and travertine thresholds and surrounds, gets dulled by vinegar. And some doors ship with a factory hydrophobic coating that acid strips. If the door is only a few years old, check before you start.

The step that keeps it from coming back takes thirty seconds. Squeegee the glass after the last shower of the day. A door that's dry within a couple of minutes never gets the evaporation cycle that builds the deposit in the first place.
localNote: Las Cruces runs on hard groundwater, and it shows up on glass faster here than in most of the country. A door that would take a year to haze somewhere else can do it in a season. If you're renting, shower glass is also one of the first things a landlord looks at on a walkthrough.

faq.q: Will vinegar damage my shower glass?
faq.a: No. Glass isn't affected by household vinegar. What you need to keep it off is natural stone and any factory coating on the door.

faq.q: How long should the vinegar sit?
faq.a: Ten to fifteen minutes, kept wet the whole time. If it dries on the glass it stops working, which is the most common reason this fails.

faq.q: What if the spots won't come off at all?
faq.a: The glass is probably etched rather than coated. Run a wet finger over it. If it still looks cloudy when wet, no cleaner will fix it and you're looking at polishing or replacement.

faq.q: Can I use a magic eraser?
faq.a: A melamine sponge is a fine abrasive and it'll take off light deposits, but it dulls glass over time. A white non-scratch pad is safer on a door you want to keep clear.
